title: Map Where AI Starts and Stops in Your Workflow in 30 Minutes
author: Joel Salinas
summary: Joel Salinas argues that leaders should keep AI agents off the org chart and instead map AI into each workflow. He cites a 2026 MIT Initiative on the Digital Economy study of 1,261 managers, in which treating agents as named employees shifted accountability away from humans and lowered review quality. His core claim is that AI cannot be held accountable, so every step it touches needs a named person who is. He offers a five-step, 30-minute method: pick one recurring workflow, list each step with one verb, label each as AI does it, AI drafts and a human decides, or human only, name who checks each AI handoff, and assign one accountable human owner. A Claude prompt helps find unchecked steps, and he shows his own writing workflow and a client marketing engine as examples. He closes by framing leaders as stewards of people, money, and technology who must understand the risks.
points: Naming an AI agent and giving it a box on the chart makes people check its work less, so accountability should sit with a human owner of the workflow.
A workflow map uses three labels (AI does it, AI drafts and a human decides, human only), and most steps land in the middle category.
The quickest diagnostic is to open the last AI-assisted email or post and ask who checked it before it went out; if no one, that is the first gap.
Anything that reaches a customer, donor, or the public should cross a line that requires the named human owner.
Even small teams can use this approach to reduce repetitive tasks and increase output while keeping judgment and accountability with people.
quotes: The study also found that treating agents like employees “shifts accountability away from humans” and “lowers review quality.
Where companies already had AI “employees,” managers checked a named agent’s work 16% less than an unnamed tool’s.
AI has no accountability. Its accountability is in whoever is using it, the company. There have to be humans who are taking accountability for that.
You can have too much AI responsibility and nobody reviewing, which is a super risky place to be.
Name one accountable owner for the whole workflow. A person, never a tool.
I know exactly where AI starts. I know exactly where AI stops. And that’s what tells me where I need to step in.
I believe that as leaders, we are stewards of what we have in front of us. That is a combination of people, resources, revenue or money, and technology: AI capital.
Put AI in your workflows, not on your org chart. Naming it and giving it a box makes people check its work less.
